newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fischler says EU pact on British cull must stand.
newsitem.headline: Fischler says EU pact on British cull must stand.

text.p: An agreement by European Union leaders for Britain to cull extra cattle must be respected before any easing of an EU export ban on British beef, the EU's Farm Commissioner said in an interview published on Friday.
Britain agreed to cull up to 147,000 cattle most at risk to mad cow disease as part of a compromise agreed at an EU summit in Florence in June for a gradual lifting of the worldwide ban.
The cull is in addition to the slaughter annually of one million cattle over the age of 30 months of age that might have eaten infected feed before it was banned.

"We agreed in Florence certain preconditions for lifting the EU ban and a step-by-step procedure for doing so," Fischler said in an interview with the Commission's staff newsletter 'Commission en Direct.'
"An essential one has not been fulfilled: this is the additional cattle cull by the UK. Before this is carried out there is no chance of proceeding to the next stage," he added.

Fischler added that the Florence agreement required the British government to prepare working documents to be studied by scientists. Only if the scientific advice was positive would the Commission start the normal decision making procedure.

On Thursday, British Ministry of Agriculture officials discussed with Commission officials a British plan to ease the ban by exempting herds certified to be free of the disease, known medically as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
British Farm Minister Douglas Hogg has said that he hopes the talks will lead to a lifting of the ban for grass-fed herds.
A Commission spokesman desribed the talks as a "preliminary, technical discussion". British officials raised the question of a regional easing but were told this was a political matter.
Northern Ireland, where there is a computerised cattle tracking system, and the Scottish islands would be the first to benefit.
"I think it is the biggest crisis in agriculture in the EU we have ever had," Fischler said, reiterating comments made in Killarney, Ireland, last month.
Even in member states where there have been no cases of BSE he said meat consumption was down on average 11 to 12 percent. Prices were 15 percent lower than a year ago.
"Our immediate interest must not be to lift the ban in the UK on cattle exports, but to lift the consumers' self-imposed ban," Fischler said.
On the cost of the BSE crisis Fischler said, "...we have no alternative but to move money from the arable sector to the beef sector."
He noted the sector was already suffering from imbalance between supply and demand before the latest BSE crisis started in March.
"The problem was that the reforms of 1992 did not go far enough," he said, adding the BSE crisis was holding up new reforms.
